extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers, magazine editors, literary critics, and anthology compilers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and procedural rules for judging, indexing, and ranking short stories for an annual yearbook/anthology (selection of 'distinctive' stories, magazine rankings, and the indexing conventions used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asterisk distinction system
rubrics_metrics.description: One, two, and three asterisks are employed to indicate relative distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three-asterisk stories are of somewhat permanent literary value. Three asterisks prefixed to a title indicate the more or less permanent literary value of a story, and entitle it to a place on the annual 'Rolls of Honor.' (Used to signal levels of distinction among indexed stories.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: The list excludes reprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only original publications during the year are considered when counting or awarding asterisks; reprinted items are not eligible for the counts and rankings shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine inclusion thresholds for comparative tables
rubrics_metrics.description: For the detailed rank tables, periodicals considered were those 'which have published during the past year over twenty-five stories and which have exceeded an average of 15% in stories of distinction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only periodicals meeting both a minimum volume (over 25 stories) and a minimum quality percentage (over 15% distinctive stories) are included in the nineteen-periodical comparative lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking guidance for ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Ties in the lists are decided by taking relative rank in other lists into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two periodicals tie on a particular metric, their positions are resolved by comparing their ranks across the other compiled lists rather than by arbitrary choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing scope and selectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories 'of distinction only' published in listed magazines and newspapers during the year are indexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index deliberately restricts itself to stories judged to be 'of distinction'; an explicit list of magazines whose distinctive stories are indexed is provided. Certain periodicals or issues not procurable were excluded (e.g., specific Masses issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author nationality notation
rubrics_metrics.description: An asterisk before the name of an author indicates that he is not an American.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing entries mark non-American authors with an asterisk immediately before the author's name to indicate nationality status in the index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abbreviations in the index
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of standardized abbreviations is used for magazine and newspaper titles in the index (e.g., 'Harp. M' = Harper's Magazine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index lists and defines abbreviations to ensure consistent, compact citation of periodicals and to aid readers in locating source publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic voice vs. imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A story should exhibit an authentic voice rather than mere imitation of a celebrated writer ('it seemed to me that I found the authentic voice of "O. Henry" speaking... Imitation of "O. Henry" has been the curse of American story-telling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitating a distinctive author's manner is generally criticized; success lies in capturing an authentic voice or genuinely developing influence into originality (example: Addison Lewis's work is praised as not being an imitator and potentially a successor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative fulfilment and contribution to folk imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A work may be judged by the degree of 'imaginative fulfilment' it realizes and its ability to add 'unforgettable legend' to the folk imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories (including verse-stories) that expand or deepen folk materials and achieve memorable imaginative effect are rated highly (example: Edgar Lee Masters' 'short story in verse' was said to realize greater imaginative fulfilment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finesse and avoidance of artificial atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Character studies should be developed 'with much finesse'; avoid a 'conventional atmosphere which demands an artificial attitude on the part of the reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story's defects may include contrived or conventional atmospheres that force the reader into an artificial stance; virtues include subtle, deft characterization and naturalistic presentation (example: Johnson Morton's 'The Understudy' praised for finesse but criticized for conventional atmosphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful rendering of personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction may derive from 'faithful rendering of a personality'—portraying characters consistently and incisively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when portraiture is unpleasant, skillful, kind, and incisive rendering of character is an admirable attribute (compares short-story portraiture to novel portraiture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresh treatment of old themes
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should be able to 'treat an old theme freshly' and 'discover in it new values of contrasting character.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality can be shown by reworking familiar material in ways that reveal new character contrasts or insights (example: Meredith Nicholson's handling of an old theme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy/simplicity as artistic strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories 'woven out of the simplest elements' and having an 'entire lack of literary sophistication' can be powerful and unforgettable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity and stark atmospheric rendering (akin to Hardy) are virtues when they produce a grim, unforgettable effect without unnecessary sophistry (example: Seumas O'Brien's 'Murder?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift of selection and focus on psychological contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinctive quality is 'gift of selection, by which [the author] brings out the most illusive psychological contrasts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting and emphasizing the most revealing details or contrasts yields psychological depth and illusion of reality (example: Georgia Wood Pangborn's supernatural stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate emotional intensity and contemporaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional quality should be 'keyed up as tightly, but as surely' as in the best work and be capable of touching 'the very heart of the experience that the war has brought to us all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional intensity must fit subject matter and era—stories that capture the current psychology (e.g., wartime psychology) and expose core experiences are highly valued (example: Lawrence Perry's story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness, restraint, and avoidance of overstraining
rubrics_metrics.description: A story should be persuasive; being 'a trifle overstrung' hurts complete persuasiveness, though artistic sincerity can still make it memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance emotional or dramatic tension to maintain persuasiveness; excess strain undermines credibility even if sincerity remains (example: 'The Portrait' by Emery Pottle described as overstrung but sincere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, unassuming earnestness, and realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, quietly told stories with 'a quiet, unassuming earnestness' render events 'very real' and promise richer fulfilment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpretentious narrative tone and earnest depiction of ordinary people can mark significant achievement (example: Mary Brecht Pulver's 'The Path of Glory').

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful folk/lowly portrayal (anti-condescension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers depicting the poor and lowly should show 'less of that condescension toward their subject'—faithful rendering of homely but real spiritual circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathetic, non-condescending representations of folk subjects are encouraged; authenticity and respect enhance the folk quality so prevalent among younger writers (example: Elsie Singmaster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reticence, subtle background rendering, and inevitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Power can come from handling tragedy 'reticently' and rendering backgrounds 'subtly' so that the action feels 'inevitable despite its character of surprise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understated narrative and finely shown backgrounds can make surprising plot turns feel inevitable, heightening emotional effect (example: Mary Synon's 'None so Blind').

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological conviction and moral/esthetic power even if repellent
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutal realism 'may repel the reader, but its power and convincing quality cannot be gainsaid'; psychological convincingness is a major merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that present unpleasant realities convincingly and with psychological truthfulness deserve recognition even if they discomfort readers (example: Elizabeth Stead Taber's 'The Scar').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial presentation of action and spiritual conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'extraordinary gift for presenting action and spiritual conflict pictorially' and a 'sense of human mystery' are notable virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to present scenes vividly (pictorially) and to fuse action with spiritual or moral complexity (including tragic humor) distinguishes lasting short fiction (example: Wilbur Daniel Steele's stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limitations and provenance in indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues or numbers unavailable through ordinary channels may be excluded from indexing (e.g., specific months of The Masses or the Little Review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilers note and justify exclusions when issues could not be procured, documenting gaps in coverage for transparency.
